pitch_detail.notes: Start from the upper SE corner of the Lower Curtis Glacier, on the snow slope below the obvious glacier tongue that reaches halfway up the face, aiming for the narrow gully at the right side of the main wall. The slope steepens to about 45° near its top and ends at a large transverse crevasse, crossed on a snow bridge; check the bridge before committing.

Above the crevasse a short band of vertical ice forms in an open-book rock corner, climbed as an ice-filled chimney in its middle, followed immediately by a second, shorter vertical step. This is the steepest ice on the route; carry a tool as well as an axe and a couple of screws.
Steep snow continues above the ice chimney to the top of the icefall. Stay in the gully line on the right side of the wall; the rock step that follows is the only way onto the glacier tongue above.

A short band of easy fifth-class rock with no protection leads from the top of the icefall onto the narrow glacier tongue. Climb it with care, likely in crampons; with no gear, a slip here would run back down the icefall.
Steep snow on the tongue leads to a second large transverse crevasse. It crosses easily on its left end; do not try to force it in the middle.

The steepest sustained ground of the lower route: ice that starts around 60° and steepens to about 70° near the top, turning to snow before the base of the rock headwall. Pickets and screws both have a place here depending on how much snow covers the ice.

At the base of the headwall traverse left to a less-than-vertical weakness and climb it on fourth-class rock to a ledge. From the ledge traverse left around a corner to reach the foot of the long buttress.

A long buttress of easy fifth-class climbing on good, solid rock with positive holds, climbed for roughly its whole height to the crest of the main SE Ridge south of the Hourglass. A minimal rack of nuts and extra-long slings covers it.
Drop off the east side of the rocky SE Ridge crest onto the Sulphide Glacier and follow it north to the south side of the summit pyramid. Rope up for the glacier; it is crevassed.

Climb the summit pyramid by the regular fourth-class line, or take a direct line of roughly 800 ft of easy fifth-class rock. In low visibility on the way down, stay high and traverse directly below the Hourglass to avoid the Upper Curtis icefall.

pitch_detail.notes: Cross the Wilson Glacier from high camp to the foot of the Thumb at about 10,200 ft. One badly crevassed area in the middle is easier to pass on a gentler ramp to its right; scout it the evening before, since the crossing is usually done in the dark. A small bergschrund marks the head of the Wilson Glacier just left of the couloir's base.

Enter the couloir just above the bergschrund, beside a steep cliff on its right side. It is narrower than the neighbouring Fuhrer Finger with a more sustained fall line; snow ranges from supportive crust to breakable crust. Be well up it before the sun reaches the rock above, as rockfall funnels into it once the slopes warm.

The couloir stays steep and narrow to its top near 11,400–11,500 ft, where it meets the Finger's line on the west side of the Nisqually Glacier. Later in the season a runnel can form in the gully bed, and hard snow can turn to ice. Avalanche hazard is real on this slope after new snow or a warm night.

Above the Thumb the crevasse-free line follows the eastern edge of the Wapowety Cleaver; the alternative traverse east onto the Nisqually Glacier is often badly broken around 12,000 ft. Expect several steep, exposed sidehill sections of 50–55° snow between roughly 12,200 and 12,500 ft above cliffs that drop to the Nisqually, easing to the cleaver's flat top near 13,000 ft.

Above 13,000 ft the slopes ease considerably but cross a field of large crevasses that can force long end-runs late in the season. Continue up to Point Success or the crater rim; for Columbia Crest, stay on the flatter ground just outside and below the rim and traverse around to the left and up onto the high point.

Two different climbs go by 'Northeast Face' on Eldorado: a pitched ice line that breaks right from the East Ridge at the bergschrund (~8,400 ft) and climbs AI3–4 ice through the schrund and face, and a set of easy-to-moderate snow traverses across the face (low line below the 8,100 ft crevasse, high line below the schrund, or a direct line above it). pitch_detail.notes: Starts on lower-angle ice just right of a large cave, in a corner roughly halfway between the Thunder Basin exit gully and the Snot Couloir — the last major weakness before the Snot. Slabby ice that is often thin, taking occasional rock gear; a mid-pitch stance lets it be split into two shorter pitches.

Thinner, steeper ice, sometimes all ice and sometimes with an occasional mixed move, climbs into the high cave (the 'snostril') beneath a huge chockstone. A full rope length or slightly more; belay inside the cave. If the crux above is not in, these two pitches still make a worthwhile ice outing with a retreat from here.

The crux: traverse right out of the cave onto an overhanging mixed wall, then finish on easier snow at the foot of a large couloir. Grades given range from WI4 M5 to WI4+ M5+ and shift with how much snow and ice has formed. Cams and screws are both needed; belay on rock on the left wall.

Climb the snow couloir above the cave at up to about 55°; parties often simul-climb the lower part. The Post Nasal Drip finish climbs the couloir's left wall above, so watch for it before continuing to the saddle.

The recommended finish is the Post Nasal Drip variation, a steep ice-and-mixed line up the couloir's left wall that often holds the best pure ice on the route. Alternatively continue up the moderate snow couloir, about 45 m, to the saddle. Top out on a western subsummit and descend a steep walk-off down the south side.

pitch_detail.notes: From the notch above Icy Lake, rope up and descend onto the Entiat Glacier, then find a short way across the ablation zone of the shrinking glacier. The crossing is trickier than older photos suggest. Skirt below the rock spur and head up toward the icefall.

Work rightward beneath the headwall through big crevasses, climbing short vertical ice steps and ramps between them; most parties move on a running belay with screws and a picket. In a big snow year steep snow slopes to one side can bypass part of the ice. The icefall has shrunk greatly and its shape changes from year to year.

Above the crevasses, gentler slopes of ice and snow at around 35° lead to the base of the rock. The rock above is slower than it looks from here; allow several hours for it rather than a quick scramble.

Turn right off the ice onto the rock, where several ramps offer a start. The rock is crumbly and protection is scarce, so running belays are the usual method. Take the line of least resistance, trending slightly toward the ridge crest.

Continue on loose fourth and low-fifth-class ground toward the crest; the rock section totals roughly 900 vertical feet and commonly takes several hours. Near the top there is a step-across at the head of a couloir. Test holds before weighting them; rockfall onto the party below is the main hazard.
A short walk leads to the heavily cairned 9,082 ft summit. Descend the South Ridge on foot, which is quick in good conditions and returns toward the Icy Lake bivy ledges.

pitch_detail.notes: Sustained vertical ice straight up the middle of Unicorn Peak's northwest face — the main event and by far the hardest ground. The fall forms only in some winters, so check it from Snow Lake before committing. There are no fixed anchors; build screw belays, and plan on V-threads for any retreat.
Much easier ice at roughly 50° continues up the face above the steep curtain. Save a few screws for the belay at its top, since about a dozen cover the whole route.

Steep rime over loose, chossy rock leads to the summit; move carefully and keep the rope clear of loose blocks. From the top, rappel the summit block and descend the south side to the col with West Unicorn, then the basin back to Snow Lake.
